The full Monte Carlo calculation gives 2.9bp - close enough for initial pricing, but they'd run the full calculation before final booking.

questions.question: How does incremental CVA differ from stand-alone CVA when adding a new trade to an existing netting set, and why might a bank's CVA desk prefer incremental CVA for charging purposes?
questions.answer_short: Incremental CVA measures the additional CVA caused by adding a new trade to an existing portfolio (CVANS+i - CVANS), while stand-alone CVA ignores netting. Incremental CVA can be lower (or even negative) due to netting benefits, and CVA desks prefer it because it directly reflects the P&L impact at trade inception.
questions.answer_long: Stand-alone CVA treats each transaction in isolation, ignoring any offsetting positions under netting agreements, and always represents a cost (negative value). Incremental CVA, calculated as the difference between the netting set CVA with and without the new trade, captures netting benefits. For example, adding a receiver swap to a portfolio of payer swaps can have negative incremental CVA (a benefit) because it reduces net exposure. CVA desks prefer incremental CVA for charging because it precisely matches the P&L impact they experience when the trade is booked - the change in their total CVA hedge or reserve. However, incremental CVA is path-dependent: it depends on the order trades are executed and changes with each new trade.
questions.why_it_matters: This distinction directly affects profitability and competitive positioning. A bank with existing exposure to a client can offer more competitive pricing on offsetting trades due to lower incremental CVA. This creates 'stickiness' in client relationships - the first bank to establish positions has a pricing advantage on future trades. Understanding this also prevents disputes between front office (who see incremental charges) and middle office (who track stand-alone contributions for risk reporting).
common_traps: Calculating stand-alone CVA for pricing when netting agreements exist, overcharging clients and losing competitive deals
Forgetting that incremental CVA depends on trade size - a small offsetting trade may show high benefit, but doubling its size reduces the benefit per unit notional
Assuming incremental CVA will remain stable - it changes as the existing portfolio evolves with market movements and maturities
questions.real_world_example: A bank has a $100MM 5-year payer swap with a corporate client (stand-alone CVA: $80K). The client now wants a $50MM 5-year receiver swap. Stand-alone CVA would be $40K, but incremental CVA is only $5K because it nets against the existing position. The bank can price in just $5K CVA charge instead of $40K, beating competitors who don't have offsetting positions. When the CVA desk books this, their total CVA only increases by $5K, perfectly matching the charge.

questions.question: What is DVA (Debt Value Adjustment), how does it create 'price symmetry' in bilateral CVA, and why is it controversial despite being required by accounting standards like IFRS 13?
questions.answer_short: DVA is a benefit arising from a party's own default risk on their liabilities (negative exposures). It creates price symmetry because one party's CVA loss equals their counterparty's DVA gain, making bilateral prices theoretically agreeable. It's controversial because the gain is difficult to monetize unless the party actually defaults.
questions.answer_long: DVA represents the economic benefit a party receives from their own credit deterioration on derivative liabilities. Mathematically, DVA = -LGD_own × Σ[NEE(ti) × PD_own(ti-1, ti)], where NEE is negative expected exposure. When both parties use bilateral CVA (BCVA = CVA + DVA), price symmetry emerges: if Bank A has EPE=100 and Bank B has ENE=-100, and both use their credit spreads, they can agree that the fair CVA adjustment is EPE × (Spread_A - Spread_B). The controversy stems from the 'monetization problem': DVA creates accounting gains when a bank's credit deteriorates, but these gains can only be realized through default (bad), transaction unwinds (requiring replacement at market CVA), or hedging by selling protection on yourself (impossible or creates extreme wrong-way risk).
questions.why_it_matters: DVA fundamentally changed derivatives accounting post-2008, causing multi-billion dollar swings in bank earnings as credit spreads moved. Understanding DVA is critical for: (1) interpreting bank financial statements correctly, (2) recognizing why regulatory capital excludes DVA benefits (Basel III), (3) understanding the evolution toward FVA as a more realistic alternative, and (4) negotiating derivatives pricing where price symmetry arguments arise. It also explains seemingly paradoxical situations where banks appear to profit from credit deterioration.
common_traps: Thinking DVA is 'free money' - it's only realizable through default or complex unwinding scenarios where replacement costs offset the gain
Assuming bilateral CVA means both parties always agree on price - they still need to agree on spreads, correlations, exposure calculations and LGD assumptions
Including DVA in pricing without considering that clients cannot generally hedge it, leading to one-sided risk-taking
questions.real_world_example: During 2011-2012, major banks reported large DVA gains as European credit crisis widened their CDS spreads. JPMorgan reported $1.9B DVA gain in Q3 2011. However, equity analysts excluded this from 'adjusted earnings' because it wasn't sustainable or cash-generating. When spreads tightened in 2013, the same banks reported DVA losses of similar magnitude, demonstrating the accounting volatility without real economic cash flows. This led to banks advocating for FVA-based approaches instead.

questions.question: Why does CVA not increase monotonically as counterparty credit spreads widen to very high levels (approaching default), and what are the risk management implications of this non-monotonic behavior?
questions.answer_short: As spreads widen toward default, CVA initially increases (becomes more negative) but eventually peaks and can decrease again. This occurs because the 'jump-to-default' risk approaches zero for at-market trades - immediate default causes no loss. This creates hedging challenges as CVA sensitivity to spreads reverses sign.
questions.answer_long: CVA exhibits non-monotonic behavior with extreme spread widening due to the bounded nature of default probability (cannot exceed 100%) and the time-value of expected losses. For an at-market swap with zero current value, immediate default causes zero loss regardless of credit quality. As spreads widen from 300bp to 2400bp, CVA increases dramatically (from -2,000 to -6,500 in Gregory's example). However, beyond extreme levels (4800bp+), CVA starts decreasing because: (1) default becomes so imminent that only very near-term exposure matters, (2) discount factors from high implied default rates reduce present value of future losses, and (3) the probability mass concentrates in the immediate term where exposure hasn't built up yet. At literal default, CVA approaches the negative of current mark-to-market.
questions.why_it_matters: This non-monotonic behavior creates serious hedging challenges for CVA desks. A simple credit spread hedge (short CDS or bonds) works well for moderate spread widening but can move against the CVA position when spreads reach distressed levels. This is precisely when hedging is most important but also most difficult. It also means that risk metrics like CS01 (credit spread sensitivity) can change sign, breaking conventional hedging approaches. CVA desks managing distressed counterparties must carefully monitor this inflection point.
common_traps: Establishing static credit hedges assuming monotonic CVA behavior, leading to losses when counterparties enter distressed territory
Using linear approximations (CS01) for risk management across wide credit spread ranges where curvature dominates
Failing to consider that netting and collateral significantly affect where the CVA peak occurs - well-collateralized positions peak at much higher spreads
questions.real_world_example: In 2008, as Lehman Brothers' CDS spread widened from 300bp (January) to 500bp (July) to 1000bp+ (September), banks with derivatives exposure saw CVA losses accumulate. However, in the final days before bankruptcy, when spreads spiked above 4000bp, some banks actually saw their CVA losses stabilize or slightly reverse, confusing P&L attribution teams. After default, the actual CVA loss realized was close to the exposure at default date minus recovery. Banks with short CDS protection experienced the expected hedge gains from spread widening but then unexpected losses in the final spike phase where CVA peaked.

questions.question: When would a derivatives user choose to calculate CVA using real-world (actuarial) default probabilities instead of risk-neutral (market-implied) probabilities, and what are the consequences of this choice for pricing, hedging, and financial reporting?
questions.answer_short: Actuarial CVA is used when: (1) counterparties lack liquid CDS for risk-neutral calibration, (2) the institution's business model is to warehouse credit risk, not actively trade/hedge it, or (3) local accounting standards permit it. However, this creates issues with fair value reporting under IFRS 13 and makes hedging inconsistent with market prices.
questions.answer_long: The choice between risk-neutral and actuarial CVA depends on the institution's business model and regulatory environment. Risk-neutral CVA uses market-implied default probabilities from CDS spreads or bond prices, creating prices consistent with hedging instruments and supporting 'exit price' accounting (IFRS 13). Actuarial CVA uses historical default frequencies (e.g., Moody's rating-based statistics), typically 3-5x lower than risk-neutral PDs, treating CVA as a statistical reserve for expected losses. Japanese banks and some smaller regional banks use actuarial approaches because: they hold derivatives to maturity rather than trading them, their counterparties lack liquid CDS, and their local accounting permits reserves-based approaches. However, IFRS 13 explicitly requires risk-neutral approaches for fair value, and using actuarial PDs creates 'Day 1 P&L' issues when transactions are immediately marked to market prices. The actuarial approach also makes CVA hedging problematic since hedge instruments trade at market prices.
questions.why_it_matters: This choice fundamentally affects bank profitability reporting, capital requirements, and competitive dynamics. A bank using actuarial CVA will report much lower CVA charges (better margins), but may face adjustment when selling portfolios or under audit scrutiny. It also creates competitive imbalances: banks using risk-neutral CVA appear to price less competitively but are actually pricing to market reality. Understanding this distinction is critical when comparing bank performance, interpreting financial statements, or negotiating derivatives pricing across different counterparty types. It's also central to the FVA debate discussed in Chapter 15.
common_traps: Assuming all banks calculate CVA consistently - methodology differences can create 50-70% variations in reported CVA
Using actuarial CVA for pricing but risk-neutral for hedging, creating structural basis that appears as P&L volatility
Believing actuarial CVA is 'more realistic' because default rates are lower - it ignores the risk premium market participants demand
questions.real_world_example: A Japanese regional bank calculates CVA on derivatives with a BBB corporate using 5-year actuarial PD of 1.1% (from rating agency statistics). Their CVA charge is 2bp per annum. A European bank uses the same counterparty's CDS spread of 180bp (implying ~11% risk-neutral 5-year PD with 60% LGD), charging 5bp per annum. The Japanese bank wins the business on price. However, when the European bank tries to buy the position from the Japanese bank, they discover a ~3bp 'gap' representing the difference in CVA methodologies - essentially the market risk premium that was ignored in actuarial pricing.
